"Ilk" means type, kind, or sort. When you use it, you are placing a person or thing into a group of similar people or things — people or things that share the same nature, character, or quality.

Think of it this way: if you had a box of red apples, green apples, and oranges, you could say "put all the apples of that ilk together" — meaning, group them by their kind.

This is the most important thing to understand: "ilk" almost never stands alone. It nearly always appears inside a short, fixed phrase. The most common ones are:

  • of that ilk — "I don't trust politicians of that ilk."
  • of his/her/their ilk — "She and her ilk have been causing trouble for years."
  • of the same ilk — "Both managers are of the same ilk — cold and calculated."
  • of a similar ilk — "This film is of a similar ilk to his earlier work."
  • of this ilk — "Scammers of this ilk target the elderly."

In every case, "ilk" is being used to say: "this person/thing, and others like them."

Here is a subtle but important point: "ilk" is technically a neutral word, but in practice, it is very often used with a slightly negative, dismissive, or contemptuous tone. When people say "him and his ilk," they are usually not being complimentary. They are grouping people together in a way that implies shared undesirable qualities.

For example:

  • "Bullies of that ilk never truly change." — dismissive, critical
  • "I have no patience for critics of her ilk." — contemptuous

However, it is not always negative. It can be used in a completely neutral or even positive way:

  • "Architects of his ilk are rare — visionary and precise." — admiring

So the word itself has no built-in negativity. The negativity (or positivity) comes purely from context and tone. Always read the surrounding sentence to understand the speaker's attitude.

Here are several examples to cement the meaning firmly in your mind:

  1. "I've dealt with con artists of that ilk before — they all follow the same script."
    meaning: con artists of that type
  2. "He, and others of his ilk, believe rules simply don't apply to them."
    meaning: he and people of his kind
  3. "This new restaurant is of a different ilk entirely — farm-to-table, intimate, unhurried."
    meaning: a different sort entirely
  4. "She had no interest in socialising with the corporate executives of his ilk."
    meaning: executives of that type
  5. "Great teachers of that ilk come along perhaps once in a generation."
    meaning: teachers of that calibre and kind

Many learners (and even some native speakers) make the mistake of using "ilk" as if it means something on its own, without a phrase around it. For example:

❌ "He is an ilk of person I dislike." — Wrong. This is unnatural.

✅ "He is the kind of person I dislike." — Use "kind" or "type" here.

✅ "He and his ilk are people I dislike." — Right. "Ilk" works here because it's inside its natural phrase.

The rule is simple: "ilk" lives inside phrases like "of that ilk" or "of his ilk." Outside of those structures, it sounds wrong and confuses people.

There is one very specific, old Scottish usage worth knowing so you are never confused if you encounter it. In Scotland, the phrase "of that ilk" is used in a technical sense in family names to mean that a person's surname is the same as the name of their estate or ancestral seat. For example, "Moncrieff of that ilk" means the Moncrieff family from the estate called Moncrieff.

This is a narrow, specialized, historical use — you will rarely encounter it outside of Scottish heraldry, genealogy, or formal family records. In everyday modern English, you can safely ignore this meaning entirely.

"Ilk" means type or kind, almost always appearing in phrases like "of that ilk" or "of his ilk," and is often (but not always) used with a slightly dismissive tone toward the group being described.

Nail that, and you have fully mastered this word.
